newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Kesri evolves from idealist to strongman.
newsitem.headline: India's Kesri evolves from idealist to strongman.

text.p: Congress party leader Sitaram Kesri, a former follower of Mahatma Gandhi who spent years as a backroom political strategist, is now calling the party's shots despite his age and formidable opposition within the party.
Kesri plunged India into a political crisis last month by withdrawing Congress' crucial support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's governing coalition.
The swift, sudden move marked a new high in a political career which has seen him evolve from a Gandhian idealist to a tactician steeped in realpolitik.
But Kesri insists that he seeks respect, not power.
As a follower of Gandhi, who led India to freedom, Kesri was jailed several times by British colonial rulers.
After a steady rise in the Congress party, Kesri, now 77, was known as "Mr Moneybags" for his ability to raise funds while keeping his personal finances above reproach.

For decades, he hovered close to the top leadership of the party as a lawmaker, minister and party official. He was Welfare Minister in prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government that lost power in last year's general elections.
His election as Congress president last September and as the party's boss in parliament in January threw the self-effacing backroom strategist into the forefront of national politics.
"Age is not with me," the veteran told Reuters earlier this year, his humility belying the toughness needed to succeed in an intraparty campaign through which he won control in parliament.

Kesri's unanimous selection by "consensus", without a formal vote, came about in much the same controversial way as the exit of his predecessor Rao, who resigned reluctantly as Congress president in connection with a bribery case.
The party reins glided smoothly into Kesri's hands, which often stretch out in affectionate handshakes that bely a tough, calculating mind behind them.
Kesri, seen as a staunch Rao loyalist, quietly asserted himself to take control from a defiant Rao.

But Rao's followers struck back after the Congress lost vital seats in a round of parliamentary by-elections this year and lost power in the northern state of Punjab to an alliance formed by a regional Sikh party and Hindu nationalists.
They loudly criticised the new president, saying that if Rao could not lead the party to an election victory, neither could Kesri.
Deve Gowda seemed to be secure in the confidence that tacit support from a weak Congress meant a longer spell in power for his United Front coalition when Kesri threw his bombshell on March 31.
Kesri has been careful, never wearing his ambition on his sleeve, and gently rallying young party supporters who give him strong backing but pose no challenge to his leadership.
He has also scrupulously avoided a split in the party. He maintained a studied distance from Rao loyalists, but never moved too close to Rao's rebellious opponents.
"People who talk about splits do not understand the Congress," Kesri said recently. "It is like a large family in which differences are sorted out collectively."
His philosophical approach has won Kesri the sobriquet of "Chacha", or Uncle, among both foes and his followers.
Kesri, whose English is faltering and whose Hindi is seasoned with rural slang, has a stature that inspires awe even among senior Congress members.

As a student, Kesri, who comes from the mineral-rich but economically backward state of Bihar, quit his studies to join the freedom movement. Jailed by the British, he refused parole to attend his father's funeral.
Many believe Kesri's roots in the movement and his amiable disposition could help him bind togther the party which led India to freedom but now finds its support dwindling.
The challenge before Kesri is to revitalise Congress, which ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947.
In a party which rivals say is too strongly oriented towards Hindu upper castes and the rich, Kesri has been an outspoken supporter of job quotas in government to help lower castes.
He also champions protection for Moslems, India's largest religious minority.
